Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

introduce verb

bring in something new

also bring in, introduce a custom, introduce a rule, introductory

classical

Cic. Tusc. 5.10: in domūs etiam intrōdūxit
Cic. Fam. 16.21.3: hāc intrōductā cōnsuētūdine
Traupman 334

intrōdūcō, intrōdūcere, intrōdūxī, intrōductum

verb, third conjugation, transitive; with in and the accusative

bring in, introduce (a custom, an idea)

Lewis & Short: “to bring in, introduce … to institute, originate”: cōnsuētūdinem intrōdūcere.

Other words

  • indūcō, indūcere, indūxī, inductum — bring in, introduce (a custom)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Rab. Post. 9 (Lewis & Short): mōrem novōrum jūdiciōrum in rem pūblicam

  • īnstituō, īnstituere, īnstituī, īnstitūtum — set up, start (a practice)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Aug. Conf. 9.7.15: ut canerentur … īnstitūtum est

    See establish.

  • intrōductōrius, intrōductōria, intrōductōrium — introductory

    declension · also used · late Latin · Cassiod. Inst. Div. 24 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 334

Examples

  • Sōcratēs autem prīmus philosophiam dēvocāvit ē caelō et in urbibus conlocāvit et in domūs etiam intrōdūxit

    Socrates was the first to call philosophy down from the sky; he settled it in cities and even brought it into people’s homes.Cic. Tusc. 5.10

  • hāc intrōductā cōnsuētūdine saepe īnscientibus nōbīs et cēnantibus obrēpit

    Now that this has become our custom, he often steals in on us unannounced while we are at dinner.Cic. Fam. 16.21.3

  • tunc hymnī et psalmī ut canerentur secundum mōrem orientālium partium, nē populus maerōris taediō contābēsceret, īnstitūtum est

    It was then that the singing of hymns and psalms after the custom of the East was introduced, so that the people should not waste away in weariness and grief.Aug. Conf. 9.7.15

See also establish, practice.
